# Tidy Isn't the Same as Right: What Happened to My Van

*This is a long one. Get a coffee first.*

---

Last Wednesday, October 28th, at about 2:15 in the afternoon, I almost burned my van down in a stranger's driveway in Bedford. Moose was on the table, half dry, and I was standing in the open side door trying to figure out which expensive thing I'd broken this time.

It wasn't the dryer. It was the wiring underneath the bench seat, and it had been quietly cooking itself for months.

Everybody is fine. Moose is fine, and honestly Moose had a great time, which I'll get to. But my van is off the road for at least three weeks, I've cancelled thirty-one appointments, rent is due on the first, and I've spent the last week doing math about amps and laying awake at 2 a.m. doing it again. So this is going to be part story and part research project, because a bunch of you have asked me the same questions and I'd rather write it all down once than answer them badly forty times.

The short version: my inverter cable was too small, the lug on the positive end was crimped wrong, and the fuse meant to save me was in the wrong place and probably the wrong type. The build looked immaculate. That's the part that keeps getting me.

---

## What actually happened

I pulled into the driveway at 2:05. Moose's mom had warned me he'd been in the creek that morning, so I was going full blast with the dryer on high, which is what I do maybe four or five times a week for a big wet dog. The water heater for the tub had been on earlier, so that was cycling in and out. This is a totally normal afternoon for me. Nothing about the day was unusual. That's the scary bit.

About ten minutes in I smelled hot plastic. My first thought was the dryer motor, because dryers get hot and motor windings smell like that when they're on their way out, and mine is a few years old. I actually crouched down and put my hand on the dryer housing looking for the problem. Meanwhile the smell was coming from *behind* me the whole time.

Then I saw it. Smoke, thin and grey, curling up out of the seam in the bench seat where the batteries live.

I want to be honest about the next thirty seconds because I think it's useful for people to hear. I did not calmly execute a fire drill. I made a noise I've never made before, hit the battery switch, and then stood there for maybe two seconds deciding whether to grab Moose or grab the extinguisher. I grabbed Moose. He's about ninety pounds and soaking wet and I hauled him out the side door and dumped him on the lawn, where he immediately rolled in the grass like this was the best day of his life. Then I went back for the extinguisher and gave the battery box a short burst. I'm not even sure I needed to. By that point the switch was off and the smoke was thinning out. But I didn't know that yet, so the inside of my van now smells like a combination of burnt plastic and the chemical aftertaste of a fire extinguisher, and the powder got into everything.

What I found when it cooled down enough to look: the positive lug on the inverter cable was black. Not brown, not "a bit dark," black like it had been in a campfire. The heat shrink around it had melted and shrunk back about three centimetres, and underneath all that neat plastic the copper was oxidized and the crimp was just a flattened mess. I could see the tool marks. It looked like it had been squeezed shut with a pair of pliers, or maybe tapped with a hammer, and then the heat shrink had been slid over it so it looked finished.

Moose's mom came out with a coffee and sat with me on her front steps while I shook. I want to say something nice about her here because it was a genuinely terrible afternoon and she was extremely kind about the fact that I'd just smoked up her driveway. She held my leash while I called my partner, and she didn't once ask me when I'd be back to finish the dog.

---

## Priya, and the part where I found out how bad it was

I got the van towed to Sackville Marine Electric, which is who I should have called a year ago. Priya runs it. She works on boats, and if you're wondering why a dog groomer went to a boat electrician, it's because a van with a big battery bank and an inverter is basically a small, badly behaved boat, and boat people take 12-volt systems more seriously than almost anybody. That turned out to be the best decision I made all week.

She spent about an hour with the van before she even talked to me, and then she sat me down with a clipboard and a pen and went through it piece by piece, patient as anything. Here's what she found, in the order she explained it to me.

### The cable was roughly a third the size it needed to be

My inverter is 3,000 watts, running off two 200-amp-hour lithium batteries at 12 volts, in a build by Coastline Van Fitouts (that's Darren) from spring 2025. The cable running from the batteries to the inverter was 4 AWG.

Priya says it should have been 2/0.

Here's the math, and I'm writing it out because I had to have it explained twice before it stuck. Watts divided by volts gives you amps. A 3,000-watt inverter at 12 volts is pulling 250 amps at full load, and that's before you account for the fact that the inverter itself wastes some energy as heat, so the real draw on the cable is higher, somewhere around 280 to 300 amps at full tilt.

Then there's what I was actually running. The dryer on high is somewhere between 1,800 and 2,000 watts. The water heater, when it kicks on, adds a few hundred more. So call it 2,500 to 3,000 watts on a heavy drying day. Divide by 12 and you get 200 to 250 amps going down that cable, and possibly a bit more with the inverter's losses.

Now, 4 AWG. Depending on whose table you use and how the cable is run, 4 AWG is good for somewhere in the neighbourhood of 100 to 150 amps in the best possible case, in open air, with high-temperature insulation. So I was running something like double to triple what that wire is rated for, not for a second, but for ten minutes at a stretch, several times a week, for a year and a half.

And I want to be clear that this isn't a "it might get a bit warm" situation. The heat generated in a cable goes up with the square of the current. If you double the amps, you quadruple the heat. Run the numbers on 4 AWG carrying 250 amps over a few metres of round trip and you're dissipating somewhere around 200 watts inside that wire. Two hundred watts is a decent-sized incandescent bulb. It's a small space heater. That's what was living inside my bench seat, wrapped in plastic loom, under a cushion, next to two big lithium batteries.

The same run in 2/0 dissipates closer to 60 watts, spread over a much bigger conductor, and that's before you get to the fact that 2/0 can actually carry the load without its insulation quietly failing.

There's a second problem too, which is voltage drop. Skinny cable doesn't just get hot, it loses voltage along the way, and low voltage at the inverter makes the inverter work harder to compensate, which makes it draw more amps, which makes more heat. It's a loop that feeds itself. Priya measured it and said it was one of the worse ones she'd seen on a van that was still driving.

### The lug was crimped with the wrong tool

This is the one that actually started the fire, in her opinion. The cable itself was undersized, which meant it was running hot, but a properly crimped lug would have handled that heat a lot better. Mine wasn't properly crimped. A proper crimp is made with a crimping tool that presses the barrel of the lug into the copper with thousands of pounds of force, so the metal and the wire basically become one piece of metal. What I had was crimped by eye with hand tools, which leaves air gaps, and air gaps mean resistance, and resistance at a connection means that spot gets much hotter than the cable around it.

So the worst heat in the whole system was concentrated in a space about the size of your thumbnail, right at the positive terminal, and it was hidden under heat shrink. That's why I smelled plastic before I saw anything. The heat shrink was doing its job in the sense that it was covering the joint, and doing the opposite of its job in the sense that it was hiding the evidence from me for a year and a half.

Priya's line, which I wrote down because it's the whole post in one sentence: **"Tidy is not the same as right."**

### The fuse was in the wrong place and possibly the wrong kind

There was a fuse, which is more than some vans have. It was a 300-amp ANL fuse. Two problems with that.

First, location. It was mounted about 90 centimetres of cable away from the battery. Priya says it should be within about 18 centimetres, as close to the battery terminal as you can practically get it. The reason is simple once somebody says it out loud: the fuse exists to protect the *cable*, and it can only protect the cable that comes after it. If a short happens in the first 90 centimetres, between the battery and the fuse, the fuse is not in the circuit. You've got a dead short across a lithium battery with nothing in the way, and that length of unprotected cable is now the fuse, and cable is a terrible fuse. It doesn't blow, it just glows and melts and sets things on fire.

Second, the type. ANL fuses are fine in a lot of applications but they have a relatively low interrupt rating, which is the amount of short-circuit current they can safely break before the arc inside them becomes a problem. Lithium batteries can dump enormous amounts of current into a fault, way more than a lead-acid bank of the same size. Class T fuses have a much higher interrupt rating and that's why Priya's putting one in. That's standard practice for lithium, and it's the kind of thing that gets skipped because an ANL fuse is cheaper and looks fine on an install photo.

Third thing, and this is the one that made me feel stupid: the fuse was 300 amp on a cable rated for maybe 130. A fuse is supposed to be the weakest link. Mine was the strongest thing in the system. At 250 amps, that fuse was never going to blow. It was just going to sit there and watch.

### There was no smoke detector in the back

There's one in the cab, which came with the van. There's nothing in the living space. So the smoke that came out of my bench seat had to travel about a metre and a half through the van before it found the detector that might have warned me, and by the time it got there I'd already had my nose in it for three or four minutes.

A battery-operated smoke detector is thirty dollars. I'll be putting two in, one above the battery box and one in the sleeping area, and I'm going to test them on the first of every month like a nerd. This is the single cheapest thing on this entire list and it's the one that would have bought me minutes.

---

## The thermal camera thing

This is the bit I keep telling people about, because it's the bit that made it real for me.

Priya pulled up the photos I'd taken of the damage on her laptop, and then she pulled up thermal camera images of her own van, running a load similar to mine, and put them side by side. Hers was a warm yellow at the worst connection. Mine was white-hot orange, and that was a picture taken *after* the fire, of damaged hardware. She had pictures of it before, too, running normally, and you could see the difference. Hers barely gets warm. Mine was running at a temperature that would melt the insulation off a wire.

The two vans are doing the same job. The difference is about six millimetres of copper and one crimp.

She also said something that's been rattling around in my head all week, which is that these failures almost never happen on day one. They happen after a year, two years, when a slightly bad connection has had time to slowly get worse, get hotter, oxidize, and get hotter still. That's why my build felt fine for eighteen months and then wasn't. It wasn't random. It was a clock running down.

---

## The money, because I know you're wondering

The repair quote is $4,200. That's a full rewire of the main runs, a new fuse block, a Class T fuse with proper mounting, and the labour to do it to ABYC standards. Three weeks minimum, and some of the parts are on order, which is the most frustrating sentence in the English language.

I've cancelled 31 appointments. My insurance is a "maybe," and the adjuster is coming Thursday, and I am trying very hard not to build a whole fantasy around that word. It could be covered. It could be partly covered. It could be a fight about whether the installation was defective, in which case it might not be my fight or it might be entirely my fight. I'll know more by the weekend and I'll write an update.

Darren hasn't answered three texts and an email. I'm putting that in as a fact and not as a character assessment. Maybe he's busy. Maybe he's freaked out. But it's been a week and it's the thing everyone asks me, so there it is.

I'm not writing this to trash him publicly. He built a van that looked beautiful, and I liked him, and I paid him a lot of money. But the cable was too small, the lug was crimped wrong, the fuse was in the wrong place and probably the wrong type, and there was no smoke detector, and those are facts that somebody else needs before they hand over a deposit. People can do what they want with them. I'm not a court and I'm not an inspector. I'm just the person whose van smoked.

---

## Tasha, this part is for you

You're about to put a deposit down with the same builder, and I know you've been excited about it, and I don't want you to cancel, and I also don't want you to do what I did, which was look at a beautiful finished interior and decide that meant the electrical was fine.

Before you pay anything, ask for these things in writing. Not verbally, not "yeah no it's all beefy in there," in writing, attached to the quote or the contract. A builder who knows what they're doing will have these numbers already and will be happy to send them. If that request makes somebody weird, that's information too.

**1. What gauge is the cable from the battery bank to the inverter, and how long is the run?** For a 3,000-watt inverter at 12 volts, you want to hear 2/0 or bigger. If you hear 4 AWG, or "it's fine, it's thick," you have my exact problem.

**2. What fuse type, what amperage, and where is it physically mounted?** You want a Class T (or MRBF, which some builders use) within about 18 centimetres of the battery positive. Ask for the amperage too, and then ask whether that amperage is matched to the cable. If the fuse is bigger than the cable can carry, the fuse isn't doing anything.

**3. Are the lugs crimped with a proper crimping tool?** Ask what tool. Ask if you can see one of the crimps before heat shrink goes on, or photos of the process. A good builder will have photos. Heat shrink over a bad crimp is how I got here.

**4. Is there a smoke detector in the living space, and a carbon monoxide alarm?** Both, please.

**5. What's the torque spec on the battery terminals and the inverter lugs, and were they torqued with a wrench or by feel?** Loose terminals are the other way to make heat. "Hand tight" is not a spec.

**6. Will you put the system in writing, with a diagram, as part of the handover?** You should walk away with a piece of paper that shows every fuse, every breaker, every cable size, and what it all protects. If you ever sell the van, that document is worth money. If you ever have a problem, that document is how you find it.

**7. Ask if they'll let an independent electrician inspect it before final payment.** Some will say yes. The ones who say no are telling you something.

None of that is unreasonable to ask. It's a few thousand dollars of equipment in a box that you live in and sleep in. You're allowed to be a pain in the ass about it.

---

## What you can check on your own van this weekend

I'm not an electrician. I'm a dog groomer who has now had a crash course at the worst possible moment, and everything below is stuff I either did myself, watched Priya do, or wish I'd done eighteen months ago. Do the physical checks with the **power off** and the **battery switch off** and, if you can, the batteries disconnected. If anything looks wrong, stop and call somebody who does this for a living. Seriously. Don't "fix" it because you watched a video.

**Get an infrared thermometer.** I got mine at Canadian Tire for forty bucks and it's the best money I've ever spent on the van. It's a little gun you point at things and it tells you the temperature. It is the single most useful tool for this, because heat is what tells you a connection is failing, and heat is invisible until it isn't.

**Do a heat scan under load.** With everything running the way you normally run it (dryer on high, kettle, whatever your heavy load is), give it ten or fifteen minutes and then point the thermometer at every connection you can reach. Battery terminals, both ends of the inverter cable, fuse holders, breaker terminals, the lugs on the inverter itself. Write the numbers down. Then do it again in a month and compare. A connection that's creeping up in temperature is telling you it's dying. If anything is dramatically hotter than the cable next to it, that's your problem child. If anything is hot enough to be uncomfortable to touch, shut it down and get help.

**Find your inverter cable and read the jacket.** Cable is usually printed with its gauge every foot or so. Find the number. Then do what I did and divide your inverter's watts by 12 to get your amps, and look up whether that gauge can carry it. If you're over, you're over, and it doesn't matter how neat it looks.

**Look at the ends of the cable.** Pull back the loom and heat shrink if you can do it without damaging anything. You're looking for discoloured copper, blackened lugs, melted or shrunken heat shrink, or a barrel you can see daylight through. Then, power off, give each lug a firm tug. It should not move. It should not twist. It should not feel crunchy.

**Check where your fuse is.** Measure it. If it's more than 20 or 30 centimetres of cable away from the battery positive, ask somebody why. There's sometimes a legitimate reason. Often there isn't.

**Check the fuse rating against the cable.** The fuse should be at or below what the cable can carry, not at or above what the inverter can draw.

**Put a smoke detector in the back.** Today. Not next week.

**Check your extinguisher.** Is it rated for electrical fires? Is it in date? Can you reach it from outside the van in a hurry? Mine was behind a bin and I had to move the bin.

**Look for anything soft or pinched.** Cable should be supported and protected, not resting on a sharp edge or squashed under a panel. Vibration plus a sharp edge equals a worn-through jacket, and a worn-through jacket on a positive cable is a short waiting to happen.

**And check your breakers and switches actually work.** Flip the battery switch with everything off and confirm the inverter really dies. Mine did, thank god, but I'd never actually tested it.

---

## Where I'm at

The van is in the shop. I'm working out of my partner's car doing nails and baths for the dogs who can't wait, which is not sustainable and also means I'm carrying a tub up and down stairs, so my back is thrilled. Rent is due on the first. The adjuster comes Thursday. I've got a notebook with a page of numbers in it that I keep looking at like they'll change.

I'm not going to pretend I'm handling this well. My whole income is that van. It's not a hobby or a side project, it's the thing that pays for everything, and every day it sits there I'm watching money not happen. I've had two nights where I did the math at 3 a.m. and then couldn't get back to sleep. If you've been texting me and I've been weird, that's why.

But the dog is fine, and I'm fine, and the van is fixable. Priya says the damage is contained to the cable run and the fuse holder and the bench seat lid, and the batteries themselves tested okay, which is genuinely lucky. And I'd rather be writing this than the other version of this.

I'll post again when the van is back and I've got real numbers on what it cost and what the insurance did. If you're mid-build or about to be, please ask the questions. Ask them even if it's awkward. Ask them twice. And go point an infrared thermometer at your battery terminals tonight, because I promise you it takes four minutes and it's the cheapest peace of mind in the world.

Give your dogs a scratch from Moose. He's fine. He's had a bath since, which he says was unnecessary.

— J.
